settings.revealHandler.label: Let other apps show files in Cmdr

@settings.behavior.revealHandler.keyword.description: Search keywords for the “Let other apps show files in Cmdr” row (settings.revealHandler.label) in Settings > Behavior > Navigation & file ops. What it does: makes Cmdr open, instead of Finder, when another app (like a browser’s downloads list) asks to show a file. Never shown. Search already matches its label and description, so add OTHER words people might type: synonyms, everyday words, any count, not a 1:1 translation. Comma-separated; no brand names, protocols, or file formats (those match in every language). settings.revealHandler.description: When another app runs “Show in Finder”, Cmdr opens that folder with the file under the cursor. Finder stays your default file manager everywhere else.

@settings.revealHandler.description.description: Help text under the "Let other apps show files in Cmdr" switch in Settings > Behavior > Navigation & file ops. Two sentences: what the switch does, then the honest limit (this does NOT make Cmdr replace Finder; double-clicking a folder still opens Finder). “Show in Finder” is the macOS command name and "Finder" the macOS file manager; use your locale's macOS wording for both. "Cmdr" is the product name; keep it. "cursor" = the highlighted row in a Cmdr file pane.

settings.revealHandler.heldByOtherApp: Currently: {app}. Turning this on hands “Show in Finder” to Cmdr.

@settings.revealHandler.heldByOtherApp.description: Status line under the "Let other apps show files in Cmdr" switch, shown when a third app (Path Finder, ForkLift, and the like) currently receives the macOS “Show in Finder” command. Says who has it and that turning the switch on takes it over. “Show in Finder” is the macOS command name; use your locale's macOS wording. "Cmdr" is the product name; keep it.

app.description: Name of the app that currently receives "Show in Finder", for example "Path Finder". Falls back to that app's raw bundle identifier (like com.cocoatech.PathFinder) when the app isn't installed any more. Never translated.

settings.revealHandler.uninstallWarning: <lead>Before you uninstall Cmdr, switch this off.</lead> macOS keeps sending “Show in Finder” here, and with Cmdr gone those clicks quietly do nothing.

@settings.revealHandler.uninstallWarning.description: Warning under the "Let other apps show files in Cmdr" switch in Settings > Behavior > Navigation & file ops, shown only while the switch is ON. macOS remembers the choice in a system-wide setting that nothing clears when an app is deleted, and it does NOT fall back to Finder, so deleting Cmdr while this is on breaks “Show in Finder” in every app until the user turns it off first. The <lead> tag makes the first sentence bold; keep the tag around whichever words start the sentence in your locale. “Show in Finder” is the macOS command name and "Cmdr" the product name; keep both as your locale's macOS spells them.

settings.revealHandler.notInApplications: Move Cmdr to your Applications folder to switch this on. From where it runs now, moving or deleting Cmdr would leave every “Show in Finder” click pointing at nothing.

@settings.revealHandler.notInApplication.description: Tooltip on the "Let other apps show files in Cmdr" row in Settings > Behavior > Navigation & file ops, shown while the switch is disabled because this copy of Cmdr is running from somewhere other than an Applications folder (the Downloads folder, a mounted disk image, or the read-only copy macOS makes for a freshly downloaded app). Says what to do first, then why. "Applications folder" is the macOS folder of that name; use your locale's macOS name for it. “Show in Finder” is the macOS command name and "Cmdr" the product name; keep both.

settings.revealHandler.notProductionBuil: Only a released copy of Cmdr can switch this on. Dev and test builds come and go, and deleting one would leave every “Show in Finder” click pointing at nothing.

@settings.revealHandler.notProductionBui.description: Tooltip on the "Let other apps show files in Cmdr" row in Settings > Behavior > Navigation & file ops, shown while the switch is disabled because this is a development or automated-test build of Cmdr rather than a released one. "Dev and test builds" means builds made while developing and testing Cmdr. “Show in Finder” is the macOS command name and "Cmdr" the product name; keep both.

settings.ai.tooltipCloud: Bring your own API key for fast, high-quality AI. Works with OpenAI, Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), xAI (Grok), Groq, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, or any local server you’re running (Ollama, LM Studio, etc.). settings.ai.tooltipLocal: Runs a small language model entirely on your device. Maximum privacy: nothing leaves your computer. Works offline. Uses ~2 GB disk space and ~400 MB memory (varies with context size). Requires Apple silicon (M1+).

"context size" ties to the local context-window setting.

settings.ai.tooltipLocalDisabled: Local AI requires Apple silicon (M1 or later). Use Cloud AI instead.

@settings.ai.tooltipLocalDisabled.description: Tooltip shown when the Local LLM option is disabled because the hardware is unsupported. "M1" is an Apple chip name; keep it. "Apple silicon" is Apple’s name for its own M-series Mac chips: use the form your language’s termbase settles, since Apple frames it in its own words in some languages. @settings.network.customTimeoutUnit.description: Unit suffix shown after the custom-timeout number input (the value is in seconds).

@settings.window.loading.description: Placeholder text filling the Settings window for the moment between it opening and its stored settings arriving. Usually invisible; on a slow disk it shows for a beat. A progress statement, not an instruction. The trailing character is a real ellipsis (…, U+2026), not three periods; keep it.

@settings.servers.card.trustedHostKeys.description: Title of the first card on Settings > File systems > Servers: the list of SSH server keys this Mac has accepted. A host key is what a server proves its identity with, and "trusted" means the user said yes to it once. Three or four words.

settings.network.trustedHostKeys.keyword: host key, fingerprint, trust, trusted, known hosts, server, forget

@settings.network.trustedHostKeys.keywor.description: Search keywords for the “Trusted host keys” row (settings.servers.card.trustedHostKeys) in Settings > File systems > Servers (SFTP, WebDAV). What it does: the list of servers whose identity (host key, fingerprint) you’ve trusted, where you can forget one. Never shown. Search already matches its label, so add OTHER words people might type: synonyms, everyday words, any count, not a 1:1 translation. Comma-separated; no brand names, protocols, or file formats (those match in every language). Chinese, Japanese, Korean: short, common words, since a query must appear unbroken in one keyword, with no typo tolerance.

@settings.servers.card.trustedCertificat.description: Title of the second card on Settings > File systems > Servers: the HTTPS certificates of WebDAV servers (usually a home NAS that made its own certificate) the user told Cmdr to trust although macOS doesn't. Two or three words.

settings.network.trustedCertificates.key: certificate, self-signed, fingerprint, trust, trusted, NAS, server, forget

@settings.network.trustedCertificates.ke.description: Search keywords for the “Trusted certificates” row (settings.servers.card.trustedCertificates) in Settings > File systems > Servers (SFTP, WebDAV). What it does: the list of servers whose HTTPS certificate you told Cmdr to trust, where you can forget one. Never shown. Search already matches its label, so add OTHER words people might type: synonyms, everyday words, any count, not a 1:1 translation. Comma-separated; no brand names, protocols, or file formats (those match in every language). Chinese, Japanese, Korean: short, common words, since a query must appear unbroken in one keyword, with no typo tolerance.

settings.servers.trustedCertificates.des: When macOS doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, Cmdr asks before it trusts it for you, and remembers your answer here. Home servers often make their own.

@settings.servers.trustedCertificates.de.description: Help text under the "Trusted certificates" card title. A certificate is what an HTTPS server proves its identity with; a home NAS often makes its own, which macOS doesn't trust. "Cmdr" is the app name and "macOS" the operating system; keep both.

settings.servers.trustedCertificates.emp: Nothing trusted yet. When you connect to a WebDAV server macOS doesn’t trust, Cmdr shows you its certificate’s fingerprint and asks.

@settings.servers.trustedCertificates.em.description: Shown in place of the list when no certificate has been trusted. Reassuring, not a warning: nothing is wrong. "WebDAV" is a protocol name and "Cmdr" the app name; keep both.

@settings.servers.trustedCertificates.co.description: Title of the confirmation asked before a trusted certificate is forgotten. A short question. Shown in a native macOS alert, so keep it to a few words.

settings.servers.trustedCertificates.con: The next time you connect to {host}, Cmdr will show you its certificate’s fingerprint and ask whether to trust it.

@settings.servers.trustedCertificates.co.description: Body of that confirmation: what changes if they go ahead. States a consequence rather than warning; nothing is lost. "Cmdr" is the app name; keep it.

placeholders.host: the server’s hostname or address, like "nas.local"

settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.descrip: Cmdr asks before it trusts a server’s key the first time you connect, and remembers your answer here. Saved servers live in the Servers list, not on this page.

@settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.descri.description: Help text under the "Trusted host keys" card title. "Servers" (capital S) is the name of the row in Cmdr’s volume switcher that lists saved servers; translate it the same way as servers.hub keys. "Cmdr" is the app name; keep it.

settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.empty: Nothing trusted yet. The first time you connect to an SFTP server, Cmdr shows you its fingerprint and asks.

@settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.empty.description: Shown in place of the list when no host key has been trusted. Reassuring, not a warning: nothing is wrong. "SFTP" is a protocol name and "Cmdr" the app name; keep both. A fingerprint is the short readable form of a key.

@settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.approv.description: Label right before the date a host key was accepted, reading as "Trusted 2026-09-07". VERB in the past tense (the user trusted it then). One word if your language allows it; the date follows immediately.

@settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.forget.description: VERB (imperative), the button on each host-key row: stop remembering this key, so the next connection asks again. One word; the button sits at the end of a narrow row. Match the wording of the "Forget server" menu item (menu.network.forgetServer).

@settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.confir.description: Title of the confirmation asked before a host key is forgotten. A short question. Shown in a native macOS alert, so keep it to a few words.

settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.confirm: The next time you connect to {host}, Cmdr will show you its key fingerprint and ask whether to trust it.

@settings.servers.trustedHostKeys.confir.description: Body of that confirmation: what changes if they go ahead. States a consequence rather than warning; nothing is lost. "Cmdr" is the app name; keep it.

placeholders.host: the server’s address, as the user typed it, for example nas.local

settings.adb.status.label: Status

@settings.adb.status.label.description: Row label on Settings > File systems > Android (ADB), naming the row that says whether the "adb" command was found on this Mac. NOUN, one word.

@settings.adb.status.foundAt.description: The status value when the "adb" command was found: where on disk it lives. Short; the path can be long and wraps after it.

placeholders.path: the full path of the adb command, for example /opt/homebrew/bin/adb

@settings.adb.status.notFound.description: The status value when the "adb" command is nowhere on this Mac. Factual, not alarming: the install line right below it says what to do. Two words at most.

@settings.adb.status.watching.description: One quiet line under the status row: Cmdr is subscribed to the Android tools and notices a phone the moment it is plugged in. Never mention the ADB server, a subscription, or a socket; a person only needs to know phones will show up.

settings.adb.status.notWatching: Not watching for phones right now.

@settings.adb.status.notWatching.description: The same line when Cmdr is not subscribed, which is the normal state when the switch is off or the tools are missing. Factual, no blame, no alarm.

settings.adb.status.keywords: status, re-check, recheck, found, not found, install, watching for phones, detect phones, connected

@settings.adb.status.keywords.description: Search keywords for the “Status” row (settings.adb.status.label) in Settings > File systems > Android (ADB). What it does: shows whether Cmdr found the Android adb tool, whether it’s watching for phones to connect, and a button to check again. Never shown. Search already matches its label, so add OTHER words people might type: synonyms, everyday words, any count, not a 1:1 translation. Comma-separated; no brand names, protocols, or file formats (those match in every language). Chinese, Japanese, Korean: short, common words, since a query must appear unbroken in one keyword, with no typo tolerance.

@settings.adb.recheck.description: VERB (imperative), the button beside the status: look for the "adb" command again, which is what a person presses right after installing the Android tools. One or two words; the button is small.

settings.adb.install.intro: Install the Android platform tools, then choose Re-check:

@settings.adb.install.intro.description: Line introducing a copyable terminal command, shown only when "adb" was not found. "Re-check" must match the button label settings.adb.recheck word for word. "Android platform tools" is the name of the download; use the wording Google’s own localized docs use. The command itself is never translated.

settings.adb.pathPlaceholder: Cmdr looks for adb the usual way

@settings.adb.pathPlaceholder.description: Placeholder in the empty "Location of adb" field, saying what an empty field means: Cmdr searches the usual places itself. "adb" is a command name; keep it lowercase and as-is.

@settings.adb.browse.description: VERB (imperative), the button that opens a file picker for choosing the "adb" command by hand. The trailing … is the single character U+2026 and means "this opens something"; keep it. Match the word macOS uses for the same kind of button in this language.

@settings.adb.pickerTitle.description: Title of the macOS file picker opened by that button. "adb" is a command name; keep it lowercase and as-is. VERB phrase, imperative.

@settings.fileExplorer.quickFilterIntroS.description: Internal setting, never shown in the Settings UI: its name in diagnostics only.

settings.fileExplorer.quickFilterIntroSe: Whether the toast that explains the first quick filter has been shown.

@settings.fileExplorer.quickFilterIntroS.description: Internal setting, never shown in the Settings UI: its description in diagnostics only.

@settings.dataWipe.card.description: Heading of a card in Settings > Updates & privacy that holds the button deleting everything Cmdr has stored on this computer. Sentence case.

settings.dataWipe.description: Delete everything Cmdr keeps on this Mac: settings, saved passwords, histories, indexes, and downloaded models. Cmdr quits afterwards.

@settings.dataWipe.description.description: Explanation under that heading, beside the delete button. "Cmdr" is the app's name; don't translate it.

@settings.dataWipe.button.description: Button in Settings > Updates & privacy that opens a confirmation dialog about deleting all of the app's data on this computer. VERB phrase, sentence case. "Cmdr" is the app's name.

settings.updates.deleteAllData.keywords: delete, erase, remove, wipe, reset, uninstall, privacy, data, forget, gdpr

@settings.updates.deleteAllData.keywords.description: Search keywords for the “Delete all Cmdr data” row (settings.dataWipe.button) in Settings > Updates & privacy. What it does: a button that deletes everything Cmdr stores on this Mac. Never shown. Search already matches its label, so add OTHER words people might type: synonyms, everyday words, any count, not a 1:1 translation. Comma-separated; no brand names, protocols, or file formats (those match in every language). Chinese, Japanese, Korean: short, common words, since a query must appear unbroken in one keyword, with no typo tolerance.

settings.dataWipe.title: Delete all Cmdr data on this Mac?

@settings.dataWipe.title.description: Title of the confirmation dialog that button opens. A question, sentence case.

settings.dataWipe.intro: Cmdr deletes everything it keeps on this Mac, then quits. This can’t be undone.

@settings.dataWipe.intro.description: First line of that dialog when the total size isn't known: what happens, and that it's permanent.

settings.dataWipe.introWithSize: Cmdr deletes the {sizeText} it keeps on this Mac, then quits. This can’t be undone.

@settings.dataWipe.introWithSize.description: First line of that dialog: what happens, how much disk space it frees, and that it's permanent.

placeholders.sizeText: the total size of everything that gets deleted, with its unit, already formatted (for example “1.2 GB”)

@settings.dataWipe.goesHeading.description: Small heading over the list of what gets deleted. Short noun phrase, sentence case.

@settings.dataWipe.goes.settings.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the app's preferences and the user's custom keyboard shortcuts.

@settings.dataWipe.goes.servers.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the network servers (SMB, SFTP, WebDAV, S3) the user saved, and the passwords Cmdr keeps for them.

@settings.dataWipe.goes.apiKeys.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the keys the user entered for cloud AI providers. "API" stays as-is.

settings.dataWipe.goes.license: The license on this Mac. To activate it again, enter the license key from your purchase email.

@settings.dataWipe.goes.license.description: Item in the "What goes" list, shown when a paid license is activated: the license is removed from this computer, and the key in the purchase email activates it again.

settings.dataWipe.goes.licenseIfAny: The license on this Mac, if you activated one. To activate it again, enter the license key from your purchase email.

@settings.dataWipe.goes.licenseIfAny.description: Same item as the license one, for when Cmdr couldn't check whether a license is activated.

settings.dataWipe.goes.askCmdr: Ask Cmdr chats and what it remembers about you

@settings.dataWipe.goes.askCmdr.description: Item in the "What goes" list: conversations with the built-in assistant and the notes it keeps about the user. "Ask Cmdr" is a feature name; keep it as-is.

settings.dataWipe.goes.histories: Recent folders, searches, and other histories

@settings.dataWipe.goes.histories.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the lists of recently visited folders, past searches, and similar histories.

settings.dataWipe.goes.operationLog: The operation log of your copies, moves, and deletes

@settings.dataWipe.goes.operationLog.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the record of past file operations. "Operation log" is a feature name.

settings.dataWipe.goes.indexes: The drive index and image search data

@settings.dataWipe.goes.indexes.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the index of the user's drives (folder sizes, fast search) and what image search learned about their pictures. The user's actual files are NOT deleted.

@settings.dataWipe.goes.models.description: Item in the "What goes" list, shown when the size isn't known: the AI models Cmdr downloaded (the local assistant and image search).

@settings.dataWipe.goes.modelsWithSize.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the AI models Cmdr downloaded (the local assistant and image search), with their size.

placeholders.sizeText: the models' total size with its unit, already formatted (for example “4.1 GB”)

@settings.dataWipe.goes.logs.description: Item in the "What goes" list: the app's diagnostic log files and saved crash reports.

@settings.dataWipe.staysHeading.description: Small heading over the paragraph saying what is NOT deleted. Short noun phrase, sentence case.

settings.dataWipe.stays: Your own files, everything on your drives and servers, and the Cmdr app itself. Data on Cmdr’s servers stays too; the privacy policy says how to have it deleted.

@settings.dataWipe.stays.description: Paragraph under "What stays": none of the user's files are touched, nor the app, nor what Cmdr's online servers hold (the website's privacy policy explains how to request deletion there).

@settings.dataWipe.cancel.description: Button that closes the dialog without deleting anything. It's the default button. Sentence case.

@settings.dataWipe.confirm.description: Destructive button that deletes all the app's data and then quits the app. VERB phrase, sentence case.

@settings.dataWipe.deleting.description: The destructive button's label while the delete runs. Ends with the ellipsis character.

settings.dataWipe.refused.operationsRunn: {count, plural, one {A file operation is still running. Let it finish or cancel it, then try again.} other {{countText} file operations are still running. Let them finish or cancel them, then try again.}}

@settings.dataWipe.refused.operationsRun.description: Shown in the dialog when the user confirmed while copies, moves, or deletes are still running; nothing was deleted.

placeholders.count: how many file operations are running, a number used only to choose the plural form
placeholders.countText: the same number, already formatted for the locale

settings.dataWipe.refused.alreadyRunning: Cmdr is already deleting its data. Give it a moment.

@settings.dataWipe.refused.alreadyRunnin.description: Shown in the dialog in the rare case a second delete was started while one is still running.

settings.dataWipe.refused.interrupted: Something stopped Cmdr partway, so some data may be left. Try again?

@settings.dataWipe.refused.interrupted.description: Shown in the dialog when the delete stopped unexpectedly before finishing. Inviting the user to press the button again.

@settings.dataWipe.doneTitle.description: Title of the same dialog after everything was deleted. Sentence case.

settings.dataWipe.doneMessage: Everything Cmdr kept on this Mac is gone. To remove the app as well, move it to the Trash after Cmdr quits.

@settings.dataWipe.doneMessage.description: Body after everything was deleted. "the Trash" is the macOS Trash; use macOS's own name for it in your language.

settings.dataWipe.partialTitle: Cmdr deleted most of its data

@settings.dataWipe.partialTitle.description: Title of the same dialog when a few things couldn't be deleted. Sentence case.

settings.dataWipe.partialMessage: A few things couldn’t be deleted. To finish, remove these yourself:

@settings.dataWipe.partialMessage.description: Line introducing the list of what's left: folder and file paths the user can delete in Finder, or keychain items.

settings.dataWipe.leftover.secretItems: {count, plural, one {One item in Keychain Access named “{itemName}”} other {{countText} items in Keychain Access named “{itemName}”}}

@settings.dataWipe.leftover.secretItems.description: Item in the list of what's left: saved passwords or keys in the macOS Keychain Access app that couldn't be deleted. "Keychain Access" is the name of a macOS app; use its name in your language's macOS.

placeholders.count: how many items are left, a number used only to choose the plural form
placeholders.countText: the same number, already formatted for the locale
placeholders.itemName: the name the items appear under in Keychain Access (for example “Cmdr”); never translated

settings.dataWipe.leftover.secretsUnread: Any items in Keychain Access named “{itemName}”

@settings.dataWipe.leftover.secretsUnrea.description: Item in the list of what's left when Cmdr couldn't check its keychain items: the user should look for them in the macOS Keychain Access app.

placeholders.itemName: the name the items appear under in Keychain Access (for example “Cmdr”); never translated

@settings.dataWipe.quit.description: The only button after the delete finished: quits the app. VERB phrase, sentence case. "Cmdr" is the app's name.
